full_judgment:
Borhanuddin J : This appeal under section 48 of the Arbitration Act is directed against the judgment and order dated 21-6-2016 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka, in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 476 of 2015 arising out of Arbitration Award dated 11-12-2014. 

 2. Brief facts are that the appellant and respondent herein entered into partnership business by executing notarized deed of partnership dated 5-2-2001 to set up a filling station under the name and style "M/s Diganta filling station" as dealer of Padma Oil Company, to buy and sale petroleum products and also for servicing and washing vehicles; Said partnership deed was supplemented by a supplementary deed of agreement dated 14-3-2001; Thereafter, both the parties executed a registered deed of partnership on 14-8-2001; It is stipulated in the deed that the nature of partnership shall be "At Will" with equal share, management of the business shall be run by the 2nd party-appellant and bank accounts will be operated under the signature of both parties. In the supplementary deed of agreement, it is stipulated, amongst others, that the respondent- 1st party will transfer half of the land out of total 11.71 katha wherein the filling station is established in favour of the 2nd party after final installment is paid to the Ministry of Works; In the registered deed of partnership, clause 6 reiterated that the 1st party will transfer half of the land in the name of 2nd party-appellant after doing necessary formalities and the Management of filling station shall be run by the 2nd party; Profit and loss will be divided equally; In clause 19 of the registered deed it is stipulated that all other matters not specifically provided in the partnership deed shall be guided by the partnership Act of Bangladesh keeping provision for arbitration in case of dispute or difference arise between the parties; Operation of the partnership business commenced in the year 2003; In course of business, dispute cropped up between the parties and as per deed of partnership both the parties gone to Arbitration. 

 3. Contention of the 1st party-respondent in a nut-shell is that respondent obtained lease of 11.71 katha land at Mirpur, Dhaka, from the Ministry of Works, Government of Bangladesh, for establishing CNG Petrol Pump vide registered deed dated 13-10-1998; Since the respondent did not have necessary fund, he entered into a partnership agreement with the appellant on 5-2-2001 for construction, establishment and running of a CNG petrol pump with equal share. It was stipulated in the agreement that the appellant i.e. 2nd party to the agreement shall be the managing partner and invest all necessary funds for construction of the petrol pump and running the business; It is also stipulated in the agreement that the respondent 1st party shall transfer half of the land in favour of the appellant 2nd party; Said deed of partnership dated 5-2-2001 has been supplemented by a supplementary deed of agreement dated 14-3-2001 executed by the parties; M/s. Diganto Filling Station was established and run as partnership firm pursuant to registered deed of partnership dated 14-8-2001. It is also contended that the appellant instead of investing own money for construction of the petrol pump, borrowed money in the name of the firm in breach of partnership agreement. Further contended that respondent repeatedly demands accounts and balance sheet of the business but the appellant did not respond; Respondent signed some blank cheques and kept those to the appellant; Instead of giving accounts of the business, appellant sought dissolution of the partnership business vide letter dated 22-3-2006; Respondent asked the appellant 2nd party to adjust bank liabilities and finalize the account but the 2nd party without adjusting account filed Title Suit No.407 of 2006 which was dismissed since registered partnership deed provides arbitration clause; Respondent-1st party instituted Arbitration Case No.668 of 2007 in the Court of learned District Judge, Dhaka, under section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001, for appointment of arbitrator to resolve the dispute; Pursuant to the order of learned District Judge dated 31-1-2008, an Arbitration Tribunal was constituted. Both the parties appeared before the Tribunal, submitted respective claims adducing oral and documentary evidence in support of their claims. 

 6. Having aggrieved by the award, the appellant 2nd party filed Arbitration Miscella-neous Case No. 476 of 2015 in the Court of learned District Judge, Dhaka, under section 42 of the Arbitration Act for setting aside the arbitral award dated 11-10-2014. After hearing the parties and perusing materials on record, learned District Judge dismissed the case vide judgment dated 21-6-2016. 

 8. Mr Prabir Neogi, learned advocate appearing for the appellant submits that on plain reading of the Arbitral Award in question vis-a-vis clause 18 and 19 of the registered deed of partnership dated 14-8-2001 makes it clear that the arbitral award has dealt with dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the arbitration and contains decision on matters beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration and thus the award is liable to be set aside under section 43(1)(b)(i)(ii)(iii) and (iv) of the Arbitration Act. Continuing his argument, learned advocate submits that as per clause 18 of the partnership deed the scope of submission to arbitration would be dispute or difference with regard to the partnership business and not regarding dissolution of partnership, as such, the award is liable to be set aside. He also submits that though clause 19 of the partnership agreement dated 14-8-2001 stipulate that all other matters not specifically provided in the partnership deed shall be guided by the Partnership Act, 1932, but Arbitral Tribunal passed the award without following provisions of the Partnership Act, as such, the award is liable to be set aside. He again submits that obligation of the 1st party and right of the second party have been stipulated in an unambiguous expression in clause 6 of the registered deed of agreement and thus failure of the Arbitral Tribunal to appreciate clause 6 and for that matter the partnership deed as a whole in it's true perspective has resulted in dealing with dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the submission to arbitration and for that reason the arbitral award contains decision of matters beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration and thus it is apparent that the award is hit by section 43(1)(b) (i) and (ii) of the Arbitration Act since the Arbitral Tribunal has stepped outside law, and it having stepped outside the law, it has stepped outside the jurisdiction. In support of his submissions, learned advocate referred to the case of SN Kabir vs Fatema Begum, reported in 66 DLR (AD) 193, the case of Central Bank of India vs Hardford Fire Insurance Company, reported in AIR 1965 SC 1288. By referring sections 7 and section 43 of the Partnership Act, learned advocate submits that in view of the above provisions of law read with clause 19 of the deed of partnership it is clear that arbitral award is hit by sections 43(1)(a)(b) and 43(1)(b)(i)and (ii) of the Arbitration Act. In this respect, learned advocate cited the case of Karumuthi Thiagarajan Chettiar vs EM Muthappa Chettiar, reported in AIR 1961 SC 1225. He next submits that the essence of a Partnership "at will" is that it is open to either partner to dissolve the partnership by giving notice and, as such, 1st party's letter dated 22-3-2006 is in essence a notice of dissolution of partnership at will and non mention of section 43 in the notice is not fatal. In this score, learned advocate cited the case of Con. Md Hashmat Ali vs Bangladesh, reported in 47 DLR (AD) I. He further submits that under the rule of law, anything in breach of law governing a certain area is in conflict with the public policy and thus the arbitral award is hit by section 43(1)(b)(iii) of the Arbitration Act. 

 16. Admittedly, both the parties gone to arbitration to settle the accounts claimed by them separately, not for the declaration whether the appellant 2nd party remains as a partner after seeking dissolution by letter dated 22-3-2006. The award passed by the arbitral tribunal is not only half hearted one but in true sense is not an award under the scheme of Arbitration Act. It is clear that the arbitral tribunal without determining the points formulated by it dealt with the matter beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration and stepped outside it's jurisdiction and thus stepped outside the law rendering the award hit by section 43(1)(b)(i)(ii) of the Arbitration Act. We are aware that claims of the parties cannot be examined in this jurisdiction. Such a course of action is not permissible in view of the fact that this court does not sit as a court of appeal to examine and reappreciate the evidence and facts of the record. But section 36 of the Arbitration Act provides that in a domestic arbitration the Arbitral Tribunal shall decide the dispute in accordance with the substantive law in force in Bangladesh. The role of the court in adjudging compliance by the Arbitral Tribunal to it's duty to decide according to the substantive law in the subject of such content. The position has been explained in the case of Videsh Sanchaa Nigam Ltd. vs Shapoorjit Pallomji & Co. Ltd, reported in 2007 (Suppl) Arb. LR 313. Relevant portion is reproduced below: 

 "It is true that section 28 (section 36 of our Act)  Arbitration Act, requires an Arbitral Tribunal adjudicating upon a matter of the present nature to decide the disputes in accordance with substantive law for the time being in force. If the substantive law is disregarded, a challenger would make out a case for interference. But if in applying the substantive law, the arbitral tribunal commits an error in its interpretation or application, unless the result shocks the court's conscience, the court will not embark on an exercise to correct the error committed by a forum which the parties preferred over the court in the first place. But it does not follow that the court presiding over the setting aside proceedings would merely see whether the substantive law was applied without seeking to ascertain law it was applied. It is here that the court's conscience comes into play so that a party who has been unconsciously dealt with in the reference may not be penalized merely because it choose a forum other than the court". 

 20. Judgment and order dated 21-6-2016 passed by the learned District Judge in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 476 of 2015 arising out of Arbitration Award dated 11-12-2014 is hereby set aside.
